accuracy.evidence: The developmental claims match the sources: pretend play typically emerges between 12 and 24 months and expands at 2 to 3; Development Matters (2021) Expressive Arts and Design lists 'start to develop pretend play, pretending that one object represents another' for birth to three, with the block-as-phone example, and 'take part in simple pretend play, using an object to represent something else even though they are not similar' for 3 and 4 year olds. Object substitution, deferred imitation and event scripts are named with their standard meanings. The Lillard et al. (2013) review is described honestly (pretend goes along with language and social growth but is not shown to be uniquely causal). The soup script is in real-life order and every prop goes to the corner where it belongs. p2, p3, m6 and m9 give whole, positive answers across every parameter value.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the adult misreadings documented in the early-years literature: treating object substitution as confusion (banana-phone item and Challenge question), stopping pretend because it is silly or messy, believing realistic toys are needed (Challenge 'only real toys' and 'must look the same' distractors), and correcting imitation as doing it wrong (Ben stirring item). For the child, the order step catches eating before cooking and the corner steps catch prop-to-role mix-ups, each with a specific reason in the feedback.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagpretend is a role-play lab: it orders a familiar event script (pan, carrot, stir, bowl), drags open-ended objects onto pretend jobs where every pairing is valid, sorts props into doctor, kitchen and shop corners, matches spoken lines to roles, and transforms one box into a car, a bed and a house. It shares no mechanic with Playing alongside and together (200) or Making a simple plan for play (423), and the lab_distinct gate passes.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step teaches one strand of the key idea by doing it: scripts (cook in order), object substitution (this can be that, one box many games), knowledge of real roles (play corners) and role language (talk like them). Wrong taps give a reason from real life ('The soup cooks in a pan, so the pan comes first'), not just a cross.

predictions.evidence: Two predictions before acting: 'Can a block be a phone in pretend play?' (tempting wrong answer: it needs a real phone) and 'Can one box be lots of things?' (tempting wrong answer: it is just a box). Both are revealed against what the child then makes in the lab.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six Challenge questions for adult and child together, each wrong option tagged with its own hint (mistake, stop, order, end, shop, cook, real, look, mess, wrong, doctor, kitchen) that names the misreading and the better idea, plus a streak counter and Another question.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and everyday words (block, box, pan, stir, coins) at an age 2 to 3 read-aloud level, four paragraphs. Adult text names Development Matters, the Head Start ELOF, symbolic play, object substitution, deferred imitation and scripts with plain explanations.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a fact, a term or a concrete mistake; the lab paragraph says exactly what the child does; the family tip gives exact objects and words to use.

mobile.evidence: Young layout with 56 px buttons, a 1.2 tall canvas on phones with large tiles, every drag also has a tap target and a button twin, and the iPhone 13 browser walk passes every step.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas aria-label is updated with every message, all actions have labelled buttons, feedback goes to a live region, text is drawn in the theme text colour on pale fills, and axe passes in light and dark themes.

sources: Department for Education (2021, updated 2023) Development Matters: non-statutory curriculum guidance for the Early Years Foundation Stage, Expressive Arts and Design (Being Imaginative and Expressive), birth to three and 3 and 4 year olds
Office of Head Start (2015) Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework: Ages Birth to Five, Approaches to Learning (Creativity)
Lillard, A. S. et al. (2013) The impact of pretend play on children's development: a review of the evidence. Psychological Bulletin 139(1), 1-34
Nelson, K. (1986) Event Knowledge: Structure and Function in Development (scripts); Piaget, J. (1962) Play, Dreams and Imitation in Childhood (symbolic function, deferred imitation)
